1.note: In this instance and in most of this chapter, the author is using the term **sons** to mean “descendants,” as in 23:28. However, in the second instance in this verse, the term **sons** is literal. Alternate translation: [And for the descendants of Aaron]

2.note: The author is using the expression **to the face of** to mean “before” or “previous to.” If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [before their father did]

3.q: וַ⁠יֶּֽחָלְקֵ֣⁠ם דָּוִ֔יד וְ⁠צָדוֹק֙ מִן־בְּנֵ֣י אֶלְעָזָ֔ר וַ⁠אֲחִימֶ֖לֶךְ מִן־בְּנֵ֣י אִיתָמָ֑ר
3.note: If it would be more natural in your language, you may want to put all the information together about who **divided** the priests into divisions. Alternate translation: [And David and Zadok from the sons of Eleazar and Ahimelech from the sons of Ithamar divided them]
The pronoun **them** refers back to “the sons of Aaron” (the priests) in verse 1. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [And David divided the priests]

The author is not referring to a specific **Thing**. He means Things in general. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could use an expression that would be more natural in your language. Alternate translation: [according to their appointments in their service] or [according to the duties to which they were appointed]

4.note: The author is using the term **found** in a way characteristic of his language and culture to mean that these **sons of Eleazar** could be found, that is, they were there. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [And there were more descendants of Eleazar]
See how you translated the term “head” in 23:8. Alternate translation: [who were clan leaders]

The author is not referring to a specific **house**. He means the houses of fathers (or clans) of the descendants of Ithamar in general. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could use an expression that would be more natural in your language. Alternate translation: [for the houses of their fathers]

5.q: וַ⁠יַּחְלְק֥וּ⁠ם בְּ⁠גוֹרָל֖וֹת אֵ֣לֶּה עִם־אֵ֑לֶּה כִּי־הָי֤וּ שָֽׂרֵי־קֹ֨דֶשׁ֙ וְ⁠שָׂרֵ֣י הָ⁠אֱלֹהִ֔ים מִ⁠בְּנֵ֥י אֶלְעָזָ֖ר וּ⁠בִ⁠בְנֵ֥י אִיתָמָֽר
5.note: If it would be more natural in your language, you could reverse the order of these phrases, since the second phrase gives the reason for the result that the first phrase describes. Alternate translation: [And since officials of the holy place and officials of God were from the sons of Eleazar and among the sons of Ithamar, they divided them by lots, these with these]

The author is using **these with these** as a common expression of his culture to mean that the Israelite leaders drew lots from a collection that included the names of the clans of the descendants of both Elezar and Ithamar. The idea is that the lots were drawn impartially, without giving an advantage to the descendants of either man. If this phrase does not have that meaning in your language, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [selecting from the descendants of both men together] or [impartially]

The author is using these possessive forms to describe priests whose work related to the care of the **sanctuary** and priests whose work related to offering sacrifices to **God**. If a speaker of your language would not use possessive forms in this way, you could express these ideas in another way. The UST models one way to do that.

6.note: Here, **face** represents “presence.” If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language, here and in verse 31. Alternate translation: [in the presence of]

6.q: בֵּֽית־אָ֣ב אֶחָ֗ד אָחֻז֙ לְ⁠אֶלְעָזָ֔ר וְ⁠אָחֻ֥ז ׀ אָחֻ֖ז לְ⁠אִיתָמָֽר
6.note: The expression **and was taken, was taken** represents the standard written Hebrew text as we have it today. This reading, however, does not seem to make sense. Scholars have proposed that a scribe may have written the last consonant of a word incorrectly. With a different consonant, this would say “and one was taken,” which seems to fit the meaning of this passage better. The UST follows that interpretation. You may want to follow the major translation in your area. Alternate translation: [One house of a father was taken for Eleazar, and one was taken for Ithamar]

6.q: בֵּֽית־אָ֣ב אֶחָ֗ד אָחֻז֙ לְ⁠אֶלְעָזָ֔ר וְ⁠אָחֻ֥ז ׀ אָחֻ֖ז לְ⁠אִיתָמָֽר
6.note: Since the author says in verse 5 that “they divided them by lots, these with these,” he does not seem to mean here that the officials alternately drew lots to give assignments to clans descended from Eleazar and clans descended from Ithamar. (That procedure would only have worked for eight rounds, after which eight clans from Eleazar would have remained without counterparts from Ithamar.) Instead, the author seems to be using an expression equivalent to “these with these”: **one … for Eleazar, and one … for Ithamar**. The idea seems to be that the assignment that went with a lot did not depend on which ancestor a clan had. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [The assignment that went with the lot did not depend on whether Eleazar or Ithamar was the ancestor of the clan whose name was drawn]

7.note: If your language would not represent a number in a form such as **first** or **second**, you could represent such numbers in a form that your language would use, here and through verse 18. Alternate translation: [lot number one … lot number two]

The author is using the adjective **second** as a noun to mean a certain kind of thing, a lot. Your language may use adjectives in the same way. If not, you can translate such adjectives with equivalent phrases, here and through verse 18. Alternate translation: [the second lot]

19.note: The author is not referring to a specific **appointment**. He means the appointments of all 24 of these clans to serve in the temple on a rotating basis. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could use an expression that would be more natural in your language. Alternate translation: [These were their appointments]
Here, **hand** represents the agency of a person. See how you translated the similar expression in 11:3. Alternate translation: [according to the regulation that Aaron their father had established]
The author is using the term **father** to mean “ancestor.” If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [their ancestor]

20.note: The author means that the **sons of Levi** or Levites whom he lists in verses 20–30 were **left** after the priests received their assignments. In other words, these are some of the Levites who were not priests. Since further Levites and their duties as singers, gatekeepers, and treasurers are described in chapters 25 and 26, it seems that the duty of the clans listed here was to assist the priests. Verse 31 seems to suggest this. You could indicate this explicitly in your translation if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [Some Levites who were not priests were assigned to assist the priests]

22.note: The author is not referring to a specific **Isharite**. He means the Isharites in general. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could use an expression that would be more natural in your language. Alternate translation: [Of the Izharites]

23.note: The author is using the adjectives **second**, **third**, and **fourth** as nouns to mean certain kinds of people. Your language may use adjectives in the same way. If not, you can translate these adjectives with equivalent phrases. Alternate translation: [son number two … son number three … son number four]

31.note: See how you translated the same expression in 23:32. Alternate translation: [their kinsmen]

The author is referring to all of these Levite clans by naming two extremes, those descended from **fathers of the head** and those descended from a **youngest brother**. It seems that the expression **fathers of the head** is equivalent to **heads of fathers**, that is, heads of father’s houses or clans, and that it indicates an eldest brother who was a family leader. The idea is that the leaders did not take birth order, and thus family rank, into consideration in these assignments. This is another description of an impartial process, likes the ones in verses 5 and 6. The UST models one way to express this meaning in plain language.

The author is not referring to a specific **youngest brother**. He means the youngest brothers in all of the clans he has listed. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could use an expression that would be more natural in your language. Alternate translation: [their youngest brothers]
